segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we know that if our earthly house, this tent, is taken down, we have a building from God, a house not made by hands, eternal, in the heavens.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in this tent we groan, longing to be clothed over with our dwelling from heaven,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: if indeed, once clothed, we will not be found naked.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we who are in the tent groan, weighed down, because we do not want to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The one who prepared us for this very thing is God, who gave us the Spirit as a down payment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So we are always confident, and we know that while we are at home in the body we are away from the Lord—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for we walk by faith, not by what is seen—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: we are confident, I say, and would rather be away from the body and at home with the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: That is why we make it our ambition, whether at home or away, to be pleasing to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For all of us must be laid open before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive back for the things done through the body, according to what each has done, whether good or bad.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Knowing, then, the fear of the Lord, we persuade people; but to God we are laid open, and I hope we are laid open to your consciences as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We are not recommending ourselves to you again, but giving you an opportunity to boast on our behalf, so that you may have an answer for those who boast in what shows on the face and not in what is in the heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if we were out of our minds, it was for God; if we are in our right mind, it is for you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the love of Christ holds us in its grip, since we have reached this judgment: one died for all, and so all died.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he died for all so that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for the one who died for them and was raised.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So from now on we know no one by human standards. Even though we once knew Christ by human standards, we now know him that way no longer.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation: the old things have passed away; look, new things have come.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And all of this is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that is, in Christ God was reconciling the world to himself, not counting their offenses against them, and he has entrusted to us the message of reconciliation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So we are ambassadors on Christ's behalf, as God makes his appeal through us. We plead on Christ's behalf: be reconciled to God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For our sake he made the one who knew no sin to be sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

notes.traditional: our earthly house of this tabernacle; the earthly tent we live in
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'our earthly house of the tent', meaning the house that is a tent. 'Tent' was a familiar image for the human body as a temporary dwelling, and Paul contrasts it with a permanent building from God. The verb 'taken down' is the ordinary word for striking a tent or demolishing a building, used here for death.

notes.traditional: in this (tent) we groan; meanwhile we groan
notes.note: The Greek says only 'in this'. Most translations supply 'tent' or 'house' from verse 1, as here, and verse 4 supports that. The phrase can also be an idiom meaning 'for this reason' or 'meanwhile'.

notes.traditional: clothed upon; to put on; be clothed with
notes.note: The verb means to put one garment on over another, and Paul sets it against plain 'unclothed' in verse 4. Most interpreters take the point to be that he would prefer to receive the heavenly body over the present one at Christ's coming, without first passing through death. How the 'naked' state of verse 3 relates to this is disputed.

notes.traditional: being clothed; having put it on
notes.note: Most manuscripts read 'having put on (clothing)', which is followed here. A few witnesses read 'having taken off', giving 'even when unclothed we will not be found naked'. Some critical editions prefer that reading as the less obvious one. The difference is a single letter in Greek.

The word is a commercial term for a first instalment that secures a transaction and commits the payer to the rest. 'Down payment' keeps both ideas: the Spirit is a real part of what is to come and a commitment to the remainder. 'Guarantee' and 'pledge', used in many versions, convey the assurance but not the part-payment.

The traditional 'not by sight' takes the word as the act of seeing. In the usage of the period it normally means the visible form or appearance of a thing, that is, the thing seen. This fits the contrast just drawn in 4:18 between things seen and things unseen. Many commentators accept this sense, though some lexicons allow 'sight' here and most translations keep it.

Most translations have 'we must all appear'. The verb means to be made visible or disclosed, not merely to turn up, and Paul uses the same verb twice in verse 11 of his life being open to God and to the Corinthians. One rendering is used for all three so the link can be heard.

The word names the raised platform from which a Roman magistrate heard cases. Corinth had one in its forum, and according to Acts 18:12 Paul himself was brought before the proconsul Gallio there. The Corinthians would have pictured a concrete place.

notes.traditional: the love of Christ constraineth us; compels us; controls us
notes.note: The phrase can mean Christ's love for us or our love for Christ. Most interpreters take it as Christ's love, shown in the death the verse goes on to mention. The verb means to hold fast or hem in, and versions vary between 'compels', 'controls' and 'constrains'.

notes.traditional: according to the flesh; after the flesh
notes.note: The Greek is literally 'according to flesh', a Pauline phrase for the merely human way of measuring things. It describes the manner of knowing, not Christ himself. Paul is not dismissing knowledge of the earthly Jesus but an estimate of him, and of anyone, by outward criteria. Several modern versions translate similarly.

notes.traditional: he is a new creature; he is a new creation
notes.note: The Greek has no verb, only 'if anyone in Christ, new creation'. It can mean that the person is a newly created being, the traditional reading, or that for such a person the new creation promised by the prophets has arrived. The wider wording about old things and new things favours the second, and many recent translations and commentators take it so. Some later manuscripts read 'all things have become new' at the end of the verse.

notes.traditional: God was in Christ, reconciling the world unto himself
notes.note: The words can be divided in two ways. One is 'God was in Christ, reconciling the world', a statement about God's presence in Christ. The other, followed here and by most recent translations, is 'in Christ God was reconciling the world', a statement about what God did through him. The grammar permits both, but the context concerns the act of reconciliation.

The word means a false step or lapse, and so a wrong done against someone. 'Trespasses' is the traditional rendering, but in current English it suggests entering property unlawfully. Some versions simply have 'sins', which hides the fact that Paul uses a different word here from the one in verse 21.

Paul's wording is deliberately stark and is translated literally. Most interpreters understand it to mean that Christ was treated as sin itself, or identified with sinful humanity, in his death. A substantial minority note that the Septuagint sometimes uses this same word for the sin offering and read 'made him a sin offering'. The parallel with 'become the righteousness of God' favours leaving the plain word 'sin'.

candidates.reason: Occurs in 2 Corinthians 1:22, 5:5 and Ephesians 1:14 of the Spirit, and versions vary between guarantee, pledge, deposit and earnest; the commercial metaphor should be the same each time.
The phrase κατὰ σάρκα and σάρξ generally recur across Paul with several senses, and whether to keep 'flesh' or paraphrase needs one policy for each sense.
Frequent in Paul and John, with versions alternating between appear, reveal, manifest and make known; repeated uses within a passage are often linked and need a consistent rendering.
Recurs in Romans 5, Ephesians, Colossians and Matthew 6; 'trespasses' now misleads and should be replaced consistently and kept distinct from ἁμαρτία.
A key word-group of 2 Corinthians and Romans (with καύχημα and καύχησις), variously rendered boast, glory, take pride or rejoice; readers need to see the same English to follow Paul's argument.
